rv.q: Within the four-square premise the level of invention and precision in this slapstick is often staggering.
Magic Goes Wrong effectively repeats the trick, even lays them open to the charge of being one-trick ponies. Yet it also takes their slapstick high-jinks to another dimension.
The whole barmy enterprise is profoundly silly — and may be too long, at two-and-a-half hours — but I was absolutely taken out of myself for the duration.
It's an amiable show that makes good use of audience participation and neatly skewers the more ludicrous reaches of the magic industry.
Magic Goes Wrong, the latest offering from the richly successful calamity gang of Mischief Theatre, is relentlessly hearty.
But the evening remains entertaining, and under Adam Meggido's direction the performers' comic and slapstick skills are on fine display.
That said, if it’s not a work of genius, then Mischief are fundamentally operating within their comfort zone, unlike their misguided recent stab at dramedy, ‘Groan Ups’.

Anyone with a sense of humour is likely to have a wonderful time and could well be exhausted by the end of an evening strong on running gags during which they will find themselves laughing for the vast majority of the time.
The show is unashamedly silly but also affectionately celebratory of a kind of variety theatre that may have long vanished -- but makes a welcome return here.
There's much to enjoy here, particularly in the interaction with the audience, and despite one or two second-half longueurs Adam Meggido directs with aplomb.

Those who love the 'Goes Wrong' brand will have a pleasant number of laughs to keep the mirth coming, but it's hard to shake the feeling that, for a large portion of the run-time, Mischief may have missed a trick.

We're at a fundraiser for illusionists who have expired in the line of duty. Sophisticato is a magician manqué, forever banned from touching his father's props until one day pater is crushed beneath them and the son inherits his mantle.
The comedy is broad as the M25 and the plot is about as directionless. But it is also very funny.
This latest show, which follows recent new play Groan Ups, confirms their transformation from impressive fringe talent who got lucky to serious global players.
